sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain the purpose of Evaluation and Management (E/M) coding and the kinds of services it reports.
- Relate the E/M service level to the documentation that supports it, including history, examination, and medical decision making.
- Describe the concepts of history (chief complaint, HPI, review of systems, and past/family/social history), examination, and medical decision making as E/M components.
- Describe time-based coding concepts and the circumstances in which time factors into level selection.
- Recognize the medical office assistant's role in gathering and supporting accurate documentation without independently assigning codes.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

E/M codes are like a label for the thinking work a doctor does during a visit — listening to the problem, checking the patient, and deciding what to do next.

### Question 2

These codes describe a doctor thinking and deciding about your care — like a detective studying clues and choosing a plan.

### Question 3

If the visit is about talking, checking, and deciding, it belongs in the evaluation-and-management bucket, not the surgery or test buckets.

### Question 4

When the doctor looks at a problem and picks a treatment, that is an E/M visit; tests like X-rays and blood work get their own separate labels.

### Question 5

Think of the three ingredients of a visit: what the patient tells you (history), what the doctor checks (exam), and how hard the doctor has to think (decision making).

### Question 6

The three main ingredients are history, exam, and decision making; counseling is an extra helper that can also matter, especially when it is the main thing the doctor does.

### Question 7

Every visit needs a short reason for coming — like the title of a story — so the record always says why the patient was there.

### Question 8

Just writing a lot does not make a tiny problem into a big one; the level should match how serious and complicated the problem really is.

### Question 9

New patient means the office has not taken care of this person for three years; if they have been seen recently, they are an established patient.

### Question 10

If the office has seen you within the last three years, you are already a familiar face, even if today's problem is brand new.

### Question 11

The code is a report card of what the doctor actually did and wrote down, not how long you waited or how happy you were.

### Question 12

The written note is the proof of what happened, and the code has to match that proof.

### Question 13

The note is the receipt for the visit, and the code has to match the receipt exactly.

### Question 14

If it is not written down, it is like it never happened — the coder can only count what is on paper.

### Question 15

If the doctor does a big job but only writes down a little, the bill can only reflect the little part that was written down.

### Question 16

Making up parts of a patient's record is lying on an official paper, and lying to get more money is wrong and against the rules.

### Question 17

Pick the level from what the doctor actually wrote for this visit, not from a pre-filled form or what happened last time.

### Question 18

You cannot make a simple problem look harder by writing more; the code has to match how hard the decision actually was.

### Question 19

An audit is like checking that the receipt matches what was actually bought, to make sure nothing is wrong.

### Question 20

The most important ingredient is how hard the doctor had to think to figure out and manage the problem.

### Question 21

A superbill is like a menu with checkboxes the doctor uses to mark what was done, so the billing office knows what to charge.

### Question 22

If you forgot to write something, add a new note that says what you are adding and when — do not erase or pretend it was always there.

### Question 23

If two pieces of the puzzle do not fit, ask the person in charge instead of quietly forcing them together.

### Question 24

If the instructions are unclear, ask the person who wrote them instead of guessing.

### Question 25

Downcoding is like saying your work was smaller than it really was, so you get paid less than you earned.

### Question 26

Upcoding is like claiming your work was bigger than it really was, which is against the rules.

### Question 27

The chief complaint is the short answer to 'Why are you here today?'

### Question 28

The HPI is the story of the current problem — when it started, what it feels like, and how it has changed.

### Question 29

HPI details are like the who-what-when of the pain: how long, what it feels like, and what makes it better or worse.

### Question 30

The ROS is like going room by room through the body asking, 'Does anything else feel off?'

### Question 31

PFSH is the background of a person's health story — what happened before, what runs in the family, and how they live.

### Question 32

The story about the back pain is the 'what happened' part, and the questions about eyes, ears, breathing, and stomach are the 'any other problems?' checklist.

### Question 33

The assistant can ask questions and write down what the patient says, but the doctor makes the diagnosis and picks the level.

### Question 34

Social history is about how a person lives — their job, whether they smoke, and their daily habits.

### Question 35

Family history is about health conditions that run in the family, like a parent's or sibling's illnesses.

### Question 36

Past medical history is the list of health problems the patient already had before today.

### Question 37

Write down exactly what the person said, like a careful reporter, and do not add your own guesses.

### Question 38

The review of systems checks lots of different parts of the body, not just the one that hurts.

### Question 39

The HPI is the detailed story of the problem, and it is one of the pieces that helps show how complete the visit was.

### Question 40

When the note asks about other symptoms like fever and cough and writes 'none,' that part is the 'checking other parts of the body' section.

### Question 41

The exam is when the doctor looks, feels, and listens to the body to check how things are working.

### Question 42

Small problems get a quick look, and big problems get a much more careful check.

### Question 43

A general exam is like a full check of the whole car, not just one tire.

### Question 44

Checking only the eyes is like inspecting just one part of the car instead of the whole thing.

### Question 45

If the doctor does not write down what was checked and found, it cannot be counted when figuring out the visit's level.

### Question 46

The assistant sets things up and writes down what the doctor says, but the doctor does the checking and deciding.

### Question 47

Write down exactly what the doctor said, word for word, and do not change it.

### Question 48

Looking carefully does not make the problem harder; the 'how hard to decide' score stays separate from the 'how much checking' score.

### Question 49

Medical decision making is the 'how hard did the doctor have to think' part of the visit.

### Question 50

MDM is scored on three things: how many problems and choices, how much information to sort through, and how risky the situation is.

### Question 51

Risk is about how dangerous the health problem is and how risky the treatment is, not about money or paperwork.

### Question 52

Risk goes from a tiny chance of trouble up to a big chance, on a simple ladder of steps.

### Question 53

The more problems to track and choices to make, the harder the thinking part of the visit.

### Question 54

Sorting through test results and other doctors' notes is part of how much information the doctor has to think about.

### Question 55

When the notes could fit more than one level, the deciding factor is how hard the medical thinking was.

### Question 56

The 'thinking work' is the doctor using judgment to figure out the problem and choose what to do.

### Question 57

An easy problem with simple advice is a light-thinking visit, not a heavy-thinking one.

### Question 58

Harder problems and riskier medicines mean more careful thinking, which can make the visit a higher-level one.

### Question 59

A brand-new puzzle takes more thinking than a puzzle you have already solved and just need to keep an eye on.

### Question 60

A management decision is the doctor choosing what to do next, like ordering a test or changing a medicine.

### Question 61

Looking at test results is more information to think about, which adds to the thinking work of the visit.

### Question 62

When the problems are hard to manage, the 'thinking hard' score matters most, even if the note is short.

### Question 63

A cold that goes away by itself is a small problem, while chest pain or a broken bone is a big problem.

### Question 64

Lots of problems plus new test results plus a medicine change is a hard-thinking visit.

### Question 65

Sometimes the level is based on how much time the doctor spent, especially when most of the visit is talking through care.

### Question 66

If most of the visit is talking through care, write down what was discussed and how long it took.

### Question 67

Newer rules count the doctor's total time working on your visit that day, not just the minutes in the exam room.

### Question 68

If you say the visit took a certain amount of time, you have to write that time down so it can be checked.

### Question 69

Face-to-face time is only the minutes the doctor is actually in the room with you.

### Question 70

Count only the real minutes the doctor actually worked on your care, and write them down honestly.

### Question 71

You can pick the level by time or by how hard the thinking was, but whichever you pick has to be written down and true.

### Question 72

The best note says both how long it took and what was talked about, not just 'the visit was good.'

### Question 73

The doctor (with help from coding experts) picks the level; the assistant supports the paperwork but does not choose.

### Question 74

The assistant helps make sure the notes are complete and speaks up if something looks off, but the doctor picks the code.

### Question 75

The assistant collects the facts and writes them down; the doctor does the visit and picks the label.

### Question 76

When you are not sure, ask the person who knows instead of making a guess.

### Question 77

Making up parts of the note that did not really happen is lying on paper, and it is not allowed.

### Question 78

Copying one person's notes into another's chart is risky because the copied parts might not be true for the new patient.

### Question 79

Write down just what the person said about why they came in, without adding a doctor's guess.

### Question 80

Finish the note before writing the bill, so the bill matches what really happened.

### Question 81

If a note is unclear, ask the doctor what they meant instead of picking the scariest or safest answer.

### Question 82

The safe rule is to bill exactly what was done and written down, no more and no less.

### Question 83

Audits are like quality checks that catch mistakes so the office can fix them early.

### Question 84

Check whether the office has cared for this person in the last three years to know if they are new or established.

### Question 85

The note explains why the visit was needed and proves the bill matches the care, like a receipt with a reason.

### Question 86

If the note is missing pieces, get the missing pieces filled in by the doctor before writing the bill — do not make them up.

### Question 87

Report the real number of minutes, not a bigger number picked to get more money.

### Question 88

The assistant can help gather and write things down, but deciding the level is the doctor's job.

### Question 89

The level comes from what was done and written for that one visit, not from how busy the office was.

### Question 90

To pick the right level, read the whole note about the visit and match the code to everything that was done and written.
